CourseName: CEN3722 - Introduction to Human Computer Interfaces

Outcomes.Text: Explain the submission processes and requirements for major app distribution platforms including Google Play, Apple App Store, and Microsoft Store.
Identify the asset requirements and metadata needed to create publication-ready app listings across different stores.
Apply review guidelines and compliance standards to prepare applications that meet platform-specific policies.
Analyze the differences between native store deployment and web deployment strategies for distributing applications.
Demonstrate the steps required to finalize an application build and package it for submission to a target platform.
Evaluate compliance considerations including privacy policies, content ratings, and accessibility requirements across distribution channels.

Topics.Title: Google Play Store Submission Process
Topics.Summary: Covers the end-to-end process of publishing an Android application to the Google Play Store, including account setup, build preparation, and listing creation.

Elements.Title: Google Play Developer Account Setup
Elements.BodyText: Before submitting an app, developers must register a Google Play Developer account and agree to the Developer Distribution Agreement.
Elements.Notes: A one-time $25 USD registration fee is required. Developers should ensure their account identity information is accurate as it appears publicly on app listings.

Items.Text: A Google account is required to register as a Play Developer.
The registration fee is a one-time payment of $25 USD.
Developers must accept the Developer Distribution Agreement before publishing.
Account details such as developer name are visible to users on the store.

Elements.Title: Android Build Preparation and Signing
Elements.BodyText: Android apps must be compiled into a release build and signed with a cryptographic key before they can be submitted to the Play Store.
Elements.Notes: Google recommends using Play App Signing, where Google manages the app signing key. Developers still need an upload key to authenticate submissions. Unsigned or debug builds will be rejected.

Items.Text: Release builds must be generated using a signed APK or Android App Bundle (AAB).
Android App Bundles (AAB) are now the required format for new apps on Google Play.
Apps must be signed with a private key that is kept secure and backed up.
Play App Signing allows Google to manage the final signing key on behalf of the developer.

Elements.Title: Store Listing Assets and Metadata
Elements.BodyText: A complete Google Play listing requires specific graphical assets, descriptive text, and categorization metadata to appear in search and browsing results.
Elements.Notes: High-quality screenshots and a feature graphic significantly improve conversion rates. Localized listings can increase reach in non-English-speaking markets.

Items.Text: A high-resolution app icon of at least 512x512 pixels is required.
At least two screenshots per supported device type must be provided.
A short description (up to 80 characters) and a full description (up to 4000 characters) are required.
A feature graphic (1024x500 pixels) is required for promotional placement.
Content rating questionnaires must be completed to assign an appropriate age rating.

Elements.Title: App Review and Release Tracks
Elements.BodyText: Google Play uses a tiered release track system that allows developers to test their app with limited audiences before a full public release.
Elements.Notes: Internal testing, closed testing (alpha), open testing (beta), and production tracks are available. Staged rollouts in production allow gradual deployment to a percentage of users.

Items.Text: Internal testing tracks allow up to 100 testers with near-instant review times.
Closed testing (alpha) and open testing (beta) tracks support broader pre-release testing.
Production releases can be staged as a percentage rollout to reduce risk.
Google performs automated and manual policy reviews before approving production releases.

Elements.Title: Google Play Policies and Compliance
Elements.BodyText: All apps submitted to Google Play must comply with the Google Play Developer Program Policies, covering content, privacy, and monetization practices.
Elements.Notes: Common rejection reasons include misleading metadata, policy-violating content, and insufficient privacy disclosures. Apps targeting children are subject to additional Families Policy requirements.

Items.Text: Apps must include a publicly accessible privacy policy if they collect user data.
Content must comply with Google's restricted content policies regarding violence, adult content, and hate speech.
Apps targeting children under 13 must comply with the Families Policy and applicable laws such as COPPA.
Violations can result in app removal or developer account termination.

Topics.Title: Apple App Store Submission Process
Topics.Summary: Covers the requirements and workflow for submitting iOS and macOS applications to the Apple App Store, including provisioning, App Store Connect configuration, and review guidelines.

Elements.Title: Apple Developer Program Enrollment
Elements.BodyText: Developers must enroll in the Apple Developer Program to access the tools and entitlements needed to distribute apps on the App Store.
Elements.Notes: The annual fee is $99 USD for individuals and organizations. Enterprise distribution requires the separate Apple Developer Enterprise Program at $299 USD per year. Enrollment requires identity verification.

Items.Text: An annual membership fee of $99 USD is required to publish on the App Store.
Enrollment requires providing legal identity information verified by Apple.
The Apple Developer Enterprise Program is available for internal enterprise distribution only.
Membership provides access to beta software, App Store Connect, and distribution certificates.

Elements.Title: Provisioning Profiles and Code Signing
Elements.BodyText: iOS and macOS apps must be code-signed using certificates and provisioning profiles issued through Apple's developer portal before they can be submitted.
Elements.Notes: Xcode can automatically manage signing when connected to a developer account. Manual signing requires creating App IDs, certificates, and provisioning profiles in the Apple Developer portal. Expired certificates invalidate previously signed builds.

Items.Text: A valid distribution certificate must be created in the Apple Developer portal.
A provisioning profile links the app's bundle ID, certificate, and authorized devices or store distribution.
Apps submitted to the App Store must use a distribution provisioning profile, not a development one.
Code signing ensures the app's integrity and developer identity are verified by Apple.

Elements.Title: App Store Connect Configuration
Elements.BodyText: App Store Connect is Apple's web-based portal where developers manage app metadata, pricing, builds, and release scheduling for App Store listings.
Elements.Notes: TestFlight, Apple's beta testing platform, is integrated into App Store Connect and supports up to 10,000 external testers. Builds are uploaded via Xcode or Transporter before they appear in App Store Connect.

Items.Text: Each app requires a unique bundle ID registered in the Apple Developer portal.
App metadata including name, subtitle, description, and keywords must be configured in App Store Connect.
Pricing and availability by region are set within App Store Connect.
Builds are uploaded using Xcode's archive and distribute workflow or the Transporter tool.

Elements.Title: App Store Asset Requirements
Elements.BodyText: Apple requires specific screenshots, app previews, and icons tailored to each supported device size in order to create a compliant App Store listing.
Elements.Notes: Screenshots must be provided for specific device screen sizes; using the largest required size may satisfy smaller sizes in some cases. App previews are optional but recommended for engagement. All assets must accurately represent the app's functionality.

Items.Text: App icons must be provided at 1024x1024 pixels for the App Store listing.
Screenshots must be provided for required device sizes such as 6.5-inch and 5.5-inch iPhone displays.
App previews are short videos (15–30 seconds) that demonstrate app functionality.
All screenshots and previews must reflect the current version of the app's actual UI.

Elements.Title: App Review Guidelines and Common Rejections
Elements.BodyText: Apple's App Review Guidelines define the standards apps must meet for safety, performance, business practices, design, and legal compliance before approval.
Elements.Notes: The most common rejection reasons include crashes and bugs, broken links, placeholder content, and privacy policy issues. Developers can appeal decisions through the Resolution Center in App Store Connect.

Items.Text: Apps must be free of crashes, bugs, and broken functionality at the time of submission.
All apps must include a link to a privacy policy that is accessible from within the app and on the App Store listing.
Apps must not use private APIs or undocumented features of the operating system.
Guideline 4.0 Design requires apps to meet minimum standards of quality and meaningful functionality.
Rejected apps can be resubmitted after addressing reviewer feedback through the Resolution Center.

Topics.Title: Microsoft Store Submission Process
Topics.Summary: Explains the requirements and workflow for publishing Windows applications to the Microsoft Store, including account registration, packaging, and certification.

Elements.Title: Microsoft Partner Center Account Setup
Elements.BodyText: To publish apps on the Microsoft Store, developers must register through Microsoft Partner Center and create a developer account.
Elements.Notes: Individual accounts require a one-time fee of $19 USD; company accounts require $99 USD. A Microsoft account is required to register. Company accounts require additional verification of business identity.

Items.Text: Individual developer accounts require a one-time registration fee of $19 USD.
Company accounts require a $99 USD fee and business identity verification.
A Microsoft account is required to begin the Partner Center registration process.
The Partner Center dashboard is used to manage app submissions, analytics, and payouts.

Elements.Title: Windows App Packaging with MSIX
Elements.BodyText: Windows applications must be packaged in the MSIX format to be submitted to the Microsoft Store, providing a modern, reliable installation experience.
Elements.Notes: MSIX packaging can be done through Visual Studio using the Windows Application Packaging Project. Legacy Win32 apps can be packaged with MSIX using the MSIX Packaging Tool. MSIX supports automatic updates and clean uninstallation.

Items.Text: MSIX is the required packaging format for Microsoft Store submissions.
Visual Studio includes tooling to create MSIX packages directly from application projects.
The MSIX Packaging Tool can convert legacy Win32 applications to the MSIX format.
MSIX packages include a manifest file that defines app identity, capabilities, and entry points.

Elements.Title: Store Listing and Asset Requirements for Microsoft Store
Elements.BodyText: Microsoft Store listings require screenshots, logos, and descriptive metadata to ensure the app is discoverable and accurately represented.
Elements.Notes: Store logos must be provided at multiple sizes. Microsoft recommends providing assets at the highest resolution available and allowing the store to scale down. Localized descriptions can be added to target specific markets.

Items.Text: A store logo at 300x300 pixels is required as a minimum for listing visibility.
Screenshots must be at least 1366x768 pixels for desktop app listings.
A short description and a full description of the app must be provided.
Age ratings are determined through a questionnaire in Partner Center.

Elements.Title: Microsoft Store Certification and Policies
Elements.BodyText: All apps submitted to the Microsoft Store undergo a certification process that checks for technical quality, content compliance, and policy adherence before publication.
Elements.Notes: Certification typically takes one to three business days. Common failure reasons include crashes, policy violations, and inaccurate age ratings. Developers receive a certification report detailing any failures.

Items.Text: Apps are tested against the Microsoft Store Policies covering content, privacy, and functionality.
Certification includes automated testing and manual review by Microsoft staff.
Apps must include a privacy policy URL if they collect or transmit personal data.
Failed certifications include a detailed report to guide developers in resolving issues.

Topics.Title: Web Deployment Strategies
Topics.Summary: Covers the approaches for deploying web applications to production environments, including hosting options, build pipelines, and performance considerations.

Elements.Title: Web Hosting Options and Platforms
Elements.BodyText: Web applications can be deployed across a range of hosting solutions, from traditional shared hosting to modern cloud platforms and static site hosts.
Elements.Notes: Popular platforms include Netlify, Vercel, GitHub Pages for static sites, and AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud for dynamic applications. Serverless hosting reduces infrastructure management overhead.

Items.Text: Static web applications can be hosted on platforms such as GitHub Pages, Netlify, or Vercel at low or no cost.
Dynamic web applications requiring server-side processing may use cloud providers such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud.
Serverless functions allow backend logic to run without managing dedicated server infrastructure.
Choosing a hosting platform should consider scalability, cost, geographic distribution, and ease of deployment.

Elements.Title: Build Pipelines and Continuous Deployment
Elements.BodyText: Modern web deployment relies on automated build pipelines that compile, test, and deploy application code whenever changes are pushed to a repository.
Elements.Notes: CI/CD tools such as GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, and CircleCI are commonly used. Zero-downtime deployments and rollback capabilities are important considerations for production pipelines.

Items.Text: A build pipeline automates the steps of compiling code, running tests, and producing deployment artifacts.
Continuous deployment (CD) automatically pushes passing builds to a staging or production environment.
Version control integration ensures deployments are traceable to specific code commits.
Rollback strategies allow teams to revert to a previous stable deployment if issues arise.

Elements.Title: Domain Configuration and SSL Certificates
Elements.BodyText: Deploying a web application to a custom domain requires DNS configuration and the installation of an SSL/TLS certificate to enable secure HTTPS connections.
Elements.Notes: Many hosting platforms offer automatic SSL certificate provisioning through Let's Encrypt. Redirecting HTTP traffic to HTTPS is a security best practice and is required for Progressive Web App installation.

Items.Text: A custom domain is registered through a domain registrar and pointed to the hosting provider via DNS records.
SSL/TLS certificates encrypt data in transit between the user's browser and the server.
HTTPS is required for features such as service workers, geolocation, and Progressive Web App installation.
Automatic certificate renewal prevents service interruptions caused by expired certificates.

Elements.Title: Progressive Web App Deployment
Elements.BodyText: Progressive Web Apps (PWAs) are web applications that can be installed on a user's device and offer app-like experiences including offline functionality and push notifications.
Elements.Notes: PWAs require a valid HTTPS connection, a web app manifest, and a registered service worker to be installable. Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools can audit PWA compliance and performance scores.

Items.Text: A web app manifest file defines the app's name, icons, theme colors, and display mode for installation.
A service worker is a background script that enables offline caching and push notification support.
PWAs must be served over HTTPS to access service worker and other advanced browser APIs.
PWAs can be listed in app stores such as the Microsoft Store and Google Play using wrappers like Trusted Web Activities.

Elements.Title: Web App Performance and SEO Considerations
Elements.BodyText: A successfully deployed web application should meet performance benchmarks and be optimized for search engine discoverability before being considered publication-ready.
Elements.Notes: Google's Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) are key performance metrics that affect both user experience and search rankings. Tools such as Google Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, and WebPageTest can identify performance bottlenecks.

Items.Text: Core Web Vitals including Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) affect both UX and SEO rankings.
Assets such as images and scripts should be optimized and minified to reduce page load times.
Meta tags including title, description, and Open Graph data improve search engine indexing and social sharing previews.
A sitemap.xml and robots.txt file assist search engines in crawling and indexing the application correctly.

Topics.Title: Asset Requirements and Store Listing Optimization
Topics.Summary: Covers the common graphical and textual assets required across all major app stores and best practices for creating listings that maximize discoverability and conversion.

Elements.Title: App Icons and Branding Standards
Elements.BodyText: App icons are a primary visual identifier on store listings and device home screens, and each platform has specific size and format requirements that must be met.
Elements.Notes: Icons should be designed on a transparent or platform-appropriate background. Avoid using text in icons as it may not be legible at smaller sizes. Consistent branding across platforms reinforces app identity.

Items.Text: Google Play requires a 512x512 pixel high-resolution icon in PNG format.
Apple App Store requires a 1024x1024 pixel icon without rounded corners, as iOS applies the mask automatically.
Microsoft Store logos should be provided at multiple sizes including 300x300 and 50x50 pixels.
Icons should visually communicate the app's purpose and maintain legibility at small sizes.

Elements.Title: Screenshots and App Previews
Elements.BodyText: Screenshots and preview videos give potential users a visual preview of the app's interface and functionality, directly influencing download decisions.
Elements.Notes: Annotated screenshots with feature callouts and promotional framing consistently outperform raw UI screenshots in A/B tests. Device frames can be added to screenshots to provide context but must not be misleading.

Items.Text: Each platform specifies required device sizes for which screenshots must be provided.
Screenshots should highlight the app's core value proposition and key features.
App preview videos should be short, focused, and demonstrate real in-app functionality.
Screenshots and videos must accurately represent the current version of the app and not include misleading content.

Elements.Title: App Store Optimization (ASO) Fundamentals
Elements.BodyText: App Store Optimization (ASO) is the process of improving an app listing's visibility and conversion rate within app store search results through strategic use of metadata.
Elements.Notes: Keyword research tools such as AppFollow, Sensor Tower, and AppTweak can identify high-traffic, low-competition keywords. Regularly updating the listing with new screenshots and descriptions after updates can improve rankings.

Items.Text: The app title and subtitle (or short description) are the most heavily weighted fields for keyword indexing.
Keywords should be researched to balance search volume and competition level.
Localized listings in multiple languages can significantly expand an app's organic reach.
User ratings and review volume are strong signals that influence store ranking algorithms.

Elements.Title: Privacy Policies and Legal Requirements
Elements.BodyText: Every major app store requires apps that collect or process user data to provide a publicly accessible privacy policy that clearly describes data practices.
Elements.Notes: Free privacy policy generators such as those from iubenda or Termly can provide a starting point, but legal review is recommended for commercial apps. GDPR compliance is required for apps distributed in the European Union.

Items.Text: A privacy policy must describe what data is collected, how it is used, and with whom it is shared.
The privacy policy URL must be provided in both the app store listing and accessible from within the app itself.
Apps subject to GDPR must implement mechanisms for user consent and data subject rights requests.
Failure to include an adequate privacy policy is one of the most common causes of app store rejection.

Topics.Title: Build Finalization and Submission Readiness
Topics.Summary: Guides students through the final steps of preparing a production-ready application build, conducting pre-submission testing, and assembling all required deliverables for store submission.

Elements.Title: Release Build Configuration
Elements.BodyText: A release build differs from a development build in that it is optimized, minified, and stripped of debug tooling, making it suitable for distribution to end users.
Elements.Notes: Common mistakes include leaving debug flags enabled in release builds, failing to update the version number, and using development API endpoints instead of production ones. Each platform has specific build format requirements (AAB for Android, IPA for iOS, MSIX for Windows).

Items.Text: Debug logging, breakpoints, and developer tools must be disabled in release builds.
The app version number and build number must be incremented before each new submission.
Production API endpoints, keys, and credentials must be configured in the release build.
Release builds should be tested on physical devices or production-equivalent environments before submission.

Elements.Title: Pre-Submission Testing Checklist
Elements.BodyText: Before submitting an app to any store, developers should conduct a thorough round of testing to identify crashes, broken features, and policy violations that would result in rejection.
Elements.Notes: Testing on the minimum supported OS version is critical, as issues on older systems are a common rejection cause. Accessibility testing using screen readers and contrast analyzers should be included in the pre-submission checklist.

Items.Text: Test all core user flows end-to-end on both minimum and current supported OS versions.
Verify that all external links, URLs, and API integrations are functional in the release build.
Test the app on a range of physical device sizes and screen resolutions.
Review the app against each target platform's review guidelines to proactively identify compliance issues.
Confirm that in-app purchases, subscriptions, or monetization features function correctly in the production environment.

Elements.Title: Version Numbering and Release Notes
Elements.BodyText: Each app submission must include an updated version number and, for updates to existing apps, release notes that communicate changes to users and reviewers.
Elements.Notes: Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is a widely adopted convention. Release notes visible to users should be written in plain language describing new features and fixes rather than internal technical details.

Items.Text: Version numbers must be incremented with each new submission; stores reject builds with duplicate version numbers.
Release notes should clearly describe new features, bug fixes, and any significant changes in the update.
Each platform has a separate internal build number or version code that must also be incremented.
Consistent version numbering practices facilitate tracking and rollback if issues are discovered post-release.

Elements.Title: Submission Packages and Deliverables
Elements.BodyText: Assembling all required files, assets, and documentation into a complete submission package ensures a smooth review process and reduces the likelihood of rejection due to missing materials.
Elements.Notes: Maintaining a submission checklist document for each platform helps teams track the status of each required asset and avoid oversights. Storing submission assets in version control or a shared drive ensures they are accessible to all team members.

Items.Text: The submission package should include the signed build file, all store listing assets, and completed metadata fields.
A link to a publicly accessible privacy policy must be included in every store submission.
Any required third-party licenses, SDK disclosures, or export compliance declarations must be prepared.
Demo account credentials should be provided to reviewers if the app requires login to access functionality.
A notes-to-reviewer section should explain any non-obvious app functionality or special testing requirements.
